title: Remembering Artists From Another Time: Robert Motherwell
author: Richard Schulman
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/0.jpeg-680x488.webp)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/24/remembering-
artists-from-another-time-robert-motherwell/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/0.jpeg-680x488.webp)

Artist Robert Motherwell.

**Truthful Fictions**

I have gazed into the lions’ eyes; the eyes of the Tsavo lions from Kenya, and
the stone Lion of Lucerne have returned the gaze. I discovered a ferocious,
stoic presence within those eyes.

Gazing into a canvas of art is like entering a palace of changelings. The best
of applied art invokes limitless dreams through a window of unfathomable
beauty. A world history of canvases reminds us that we are never truly alone.

I gazed into the eyes of a 25-foot reticulated python, caressing her neck once
or twice as she returned my gaze. I have shaken the hands of Hollywood’s
Golden Age, and they gazed back in return. I have gazed into the temples of
art greatness–Noguchi and de Kooning come to mind. I have walked in the
corridors and communities of art history, visiting nearly 1000 artists’
studios and nearly 100 museums. Faces come at me like ghosts in the daylight.
I remember them like the card game _War_ : a game that is not strategically
complicated. You flip one towards your opponent, and impatiently wait for the
challenging return. My archives house the lives of so many ghosts.

I have experienced a good number of “infectious trifectas”–artists I have
photographed three separate times, including Kelly, Lichtenstein, Johns,
Botero, Rauschenberg and more. Returning to these familiar landscapes is
exhilarating; sometimes a mere few hours becomes a reverie of artful, soulful
moments.

The artist Robert Motherwell was waiting for me in his studio. Crossing that
threshold was like stepping into a giant diorama. I was the shapeshifter
straddling generational worlds that separate ages and movements. My brain
became the ball in an arcade pinball game, bouncing from a young burgeoning
Keith Haring to Robert Motherwell-from emerging Graffiti art back in time to
Abstract Expressionism and Surrealism. Historical entries appeared in my
illusory imagining, walking with giants.

![](https://images.squarespace-
cdn.com/content/v1/5877d74f725e2540a2f2c4d7/9401db62-63e2-48a3-b948-941087b0209d/0-1.jpeg)

Artist Robert Motherwell.

Robert Motherwell was older than I imagined. Through my cameras’ captures, a
living embodiment of twentieth-century art history greeted me. In one of two
guises: ”Let’s get this over with, or, let’s talk and enjoy the meeting of our
decidedly divided ages ”. Fortunately for me, three or so hours flew by.

Just about every artist I met started the conversations with, “I hear you
photographed Bill de Kooning”. I knew then that it was a generous calling
card. From there, no question whether inane or curious was inappropriate. So
after the de Kooning briefing and a few niceties, the great artist took me by
the shoulder and escorted me around the studio without a word spoken. I felt
as though i was navigating a parallax view. The world and my eyes shifted with
different curious pronouncements happening as one.

I spotted a reproduction of his Elegies series. I saw a black painting that
reminded me of Sargent’s Spanish Flamenco series. I asked about the
influences. He said, “Maybe we should sit for a while.” He started by saying,
“I thought you came here to shoot my portrait.” The Motherwell monologue after
that was a great series of run-on sentences.

He spoke about familiar stories-the damnation of being forced to emulate
Cezanne in art school. He whispered with eyes looking in many directions, that
he might have at times had Sargent in his mind. Then we shifted the
conversation to his friendships and my art world captures. We had Kenneth
Noland, Helen Frankenthaler, Matta, Clement Greenberg in common. Though as we
danced in periods of commonality, we touched on Ernst, Dali, de Kooning and
ten more. The hours were a classroom symposium on thrills and more.

He looked at his watch and I knew a good time, a great education was nearing
the finish line…so I began to shoot.

Some artists live their lives in three stages: small and intimate spaces;
large spaces to create a larger identity; and a less imposing space that
tethers the future and the past. Motherwell in this immense carriage house was
in the “tethering” phase-a tremendous home, and an intimate serenade to the
past and what may be the future. Connecticut was not Paris or New York. As I
caressed his paintings, I felt a dance come over me. Maybe a Maypole, yet a
jig nonetheless. Round and round we go, dancing on the moments of space and
time. My time will never have a fixed place in history; from near and far it
appears like a tiny ball of yarn, unraveling pieces of my history. The
passionate sharing between two generations seems quite sumptuous in hindsight.
